Forest Fire Management Research Dashboard

Summary of 5 key papers on wildfire prevention, detection, and management

Cross-Paper Key Themes

Human-Induced Causes

Primary driver of fires (e.g., Mahua collection in Odisha, agricultural burns, accidental ignition) – emphasized in all papers.

Technology Integration

Use of IoT sensors (temperature/smoke), satellite imagery (Landsat/Sentinel-2), drones, and cloud storage for monitoring/detection.

Community Engagement

Critical for prevention (awareness campaigns) and early response – highlighted in India-wide models and Himalayan studies.

Regional Vulnerability

Himalayan regions (Uttarakhand/Himachal) and Odisha face unique risks: Chir Pine flammability, NTFP collection, and climate factors.

Post-Fire Management

Includes severity assessment (NBR/dNBR), rehabilitation, erosion control, and restoration planning – critical for ecosystem recovery.

Policy & Framework

Need for national (NAPFF) and state-level policies, funding, and capacity building (training, equipment) – stressed in Indian models.

Disagreements/Contradictions

No major disagreements across papers – findings are largely complementary. Minor nuances include:

  • Paper 01 promotes prescribed burning as a management tool, while Paper 03 highlights the flammability of Chir Pine (a key species in Himalayan fires) – this is complementary (prescribed burning requires careful regulation in fire-prone areas).
  • Paper 05 focuses on a specific NTFP cause (Mahua collection), while others discuss broader human causes – no conflict, as NTFP collection is a subset of anthropogenic risks.

Paper Summaries

01: Forest Fire Models in India

  • Documents 3 management models: Prescribed Burning, Fire Suppression, Community-Based.
  • Emphasizes prevention (fire breaks, awareness), detection (satellites/drones), and post-fire rehab.
  • Highlights policy gaps (funding, dedicated fire units) and need for capacity building.

03: Himalayan Forest Fires

  • Chir Pine dominance and human activity (intentional/accidental) are primary drivers.
  • Severe impacts: biodiversity loss, soil erosion, carbon emissions (3.3M tons/year in Nepal).
  • Uttarakhand/Himachal Pradesh most affected – links to climate change and fuel accumulation.

09: Uttarakhand Burn Severity (2024)

  • Uses Landsat-8/9 and Sentinel-2 with NBR/dNBR to map severity (high/moderate/low).
  • High severity in pine-dominated areas; moderate in mixed forests; low in sparse vegetation.
  • Supports post-fire planning (reforestation, erosion control) and long-term risk management.

11: Cloud-IoT Fire Alert System

  • Proposes IoT sensors (temperature, smoke) + Arduino + cloud storage for early detection.
  • Alerts forest officers and communities via Bluetooth/LCD – real-time monitoring.
  • Aims to reduce fire spread by enabling rapid response to early ignition.

16: Madhuca longifolia as Fire Cause

  • Mahua flower collection (NTFP) is a major fire cause in Odisha – locals burn dry leaves to access flowers.
  • Tree has ecological (hosts orchids), food, medicinal, and economic values.
  • Calls for sustainable collection practices (no fire) and value addition to reduce fire risk.
